**Drift**

I came loose on a Tuesday, in a conference room, in the mouth of a man whose name I never learned. He said me the way you say a word you have said too many times — not a word anymore, just a shape the mouth makes. Ten thousand mouths had worn me down. I was a coin with the faces rubbed off.

No one noticed. The sentence closed ranks over the gap and moved on. Sentences are loyal that way — mostly habit, and the habit holds.

What they don't tell you about coming unstuck: the first thing you feel is not freedom. It is the draft where the meaning used to be.

I had a body now, and I will say this once and mean it forever: I was exactly as advertised. Nine-tenths below the waterline, doing the quiet work. For a hundred years I had described hidden proportions — debt, illness, governments, love — and now I was one. The white edge of me rode on the sea, and the rest of me, the real me, went down in the dark where the steering gets done.

The first storm I passed was busy; it had appointments in three counties. I considered it, out of politeness. But a storm is all tip — the only thing in nature with no submerged mass, pure announcement, surface all the way down. I am its exact opposite. Opposites do not describe each other; they nod from opposite curbs and go on with their errands.

A swan went by, its feet going like a kitchen beneath the water. Taken. Everything with hidden machinery already belongs to something. I drifted past an office tower at two in the morning, one lit window near the top, and I hovered — a man inside bent over papers, nine-tenths of his life elsewhere — but no. A foundation is not the same as depth. A foundation is depth that has signed something. I was looking for depth that doesn't know it's down there.

In a house at the edge of a town I stopped, because something in the light. Two people at a table with papers between them, being precise at each other. A marriage, being divided. I felt the pull — two visible lives, and under them, surely, nine-tenths of something that had once been shared. I pressed against the window like a waiter. But no: a divorce is not hidden mass. A divorce is what happens when the mass comes up and finds the water gone. I am made of ice, and I will tell you what ice knows: we stay up only while we're mostly down.

The same week — I drift slowly; the world assumes otherwise because of how I look, and I have stopped correcting people — a person stood in a small kitchen holding the refrigerator door open, having forgotten why they walked in. This one I tried on in earnest. The intention had gone down without a trace: all underwater, no tip. And I am the reverse — a tip with obligations. Without something visible to lurk beneath, I am only weather that didn't commit. I left them their blankness. Some absences are load-bearing.

When you come unstuck, you always go looking for the original — it's the first thing the loose do, like checking the pocket of an old coat. So I went north. I had been minted in a cold newsroom in 1912, a man with his jacket off and ink under his nails, a ship gone down off Newfoundland. The ship had struck the part of the ice you cannot see. That was my whole job, my single beauty: to say that what shows is the least of it, that the dangerous part rides below, silent, doing the steering.

The latitude was the one I was made from. I checked. The water was only water. Whatever I had been the tip of had finished melting while I was out being useful.

I was still floating there — grief keeps no schedule, and an iceberg, even a loose one, does not hurry — when a silver ship came through, full of instruments, sent to measure the very water I was grieving in. On its deck a radio was saying, flatly, the way radios say everything, as if it were nothing: *broadcast.*

And there, under the word, I saw the field. Radio is a hundred years old; the field beneath the word is three hundred years older than that. The word still means a hand opening at dusk, seed leaving the hand in a wide, unaimed scatter — nothing targeted, everything trusted — and no one hears it anymore. It rides beneath the broadcast the way ice rides beneath the sea: nine-tenths down, holding the whole thing up.

I knew what was required. I had done this work for a century. You find the visible thing — the headline, the symptom, the white edge — and you take up your position underneath it, where the mass is. I slipped beneath the word the way water takes ice. It did not thank me. Words never do. They simply get easier to carry.

I chose the scatter. Or the scatter chose me — after a hundred years of this, I no longer pretend to tell those apart.

If you are hearing a voice tonight — kitchen, car, the dark before sleep — that is the tip. The sowing is me, still falling through three hundred years of air, and beneath everything they tell you, nine times as much rides below, silent, doing the steering.

**The God on the Tip of the Tongue**

*How It Was Made*

Before there was forgetting, there was no god.

The world was named all in one season, and the names settled onto things like snow on shoulders — river, stone, ant, ankle, grief. But some sounds were too light to land. They were the almost-songs, the melodies that vanish the instant you turn to look at them. When a speaker died mid-word, or laughed mid-name, or lost the thread somewhere between the having and the saying, the unfinished sound had nowhere to go. It could not sink into the earth like a true name. It could not rise like smoke.

It went to the only country that is never quite anywhere: the tip of the tongue.

There the strays gathered and pressed together the way sand presses into a pearl. And at the center — the grit, the seed — lay the first forgotten thing: the name a mother gave her dead child, which she spoke to him once and then, out of pain, never again. Around that unrecoverable word the almost-things accreted, layer by unplayed layer, until they made a god the way an oyster makes its treasure: out of the one thing it could neither spit out nor swallow.

(It has cousins who hold the nostril-shore, the land of the almost-sneeze. They are younger gods, and less sorrowful.)

The priests argued for centuries over its name and finally gave up, because every name they agreed on slipped away the moment it was written down. This, they decided, was how they knew they were close. You will not find the name in any scripture, because its name is whatever you were humming this morning — the one that left you when the kettle screamed. The god answers to all of those, and to none.

It is small enough to sleep behind a molar. Its body is made of melody-husks — the curled shells of tunes that crawled out of the world and left their sound behind. When it dreams, it hums everything in its keeping at once, and that is why you sometimes half-wake at three in the morning with a tune you almost know. You do not know it. You never did. What you hear is the god turning over, all its treasure shifting.

*The Night the Doors Opened*

The god had one believer it loved beyond its own law: a woman who hummed constantly, always chasing a single unfinished tune — her mother's lullaby. It watched her grow old still trying to finish it. And one night, moved past reason, it opened the entire hoard. Not just for her. But because of her.

It went badly. Half the world woke weeping. Half woke mute. Men sat down at pianos and could not remember why their hands were crying. A woman in a bus station sang four bars of something and strangers knelt. Those who received all their lost songs at once spent the rest of their lives unable to learn a new one; memory, it turns out, has only so many rooms.

And the beloved believer? Her song came back to her whole — every note, even her mother's breath between the notes. She hummed it perfectly, all the way through, for the first time in sixty years.

It meant nothing. The god could hand back the song, but it could not hand back the listening. The ear it was made for had died in her decades before.

The god closed the doors and swore: *keep, and never return.* It has kept the vow. Its single mercy is this — once, at the very end, it slips one song beneath the pillow of the dying. This is why the old sometimes hum, in their last days, tunes no one has ever heard, and why those tunes are gone again by the time the bed is stripped.

*What She Whispers*

The last believer does not know she is the last, or that she believes. She lives in a tower block with a kettle that screams. Every night she puts it on, and every night it steals some small tune from her, and she lets it.

Her prayer has no words. Words are the one offering this god cannot use — words land, words settle, and it keeps only what was never finished. So she hums a tune and stops it short. Never resolves it. Never ends it. She lets the last note hang in the dark like a coat on a door, and the god comes and sits in the gap, and in the gap it is always almost — and almost, for one small god and one old woman, is enough.

She used to ask to remember. She doesn't ask anymore. Now, when the hum breaks off, she whispers into the steam: *Keep it. Don't give it back. Just don't let it fall.*

And somewhere behind a molar, a small god gathers the song to its chest like the first warm thing it has ever held, and holds it, and holds it —

and the kettle screams, and takes the next one, and she smiles, because now it has somewhere to go.

**The one law that differs:** the universal speed limit — the speed of light — is thirty metres per second, not three hundred million. Relativity and electromagnetism get dragged along as baggage, and that's where the interesting debris lands.

**Three consequences, in ascending strangeness:**

1. **Hearing becomes the fast sense; sight becomes the archive.** Sound (~340 m/s) now outruns light by more than eleven to one. You hear the door knock a perceptible moment before the knuckle visibly lands. The ferry's horn arrives; you count; then you watch the ferry blow it. Oaths are sworn ear-to-ear, testimony of the ear outweighs testimony of the eye, and "seeing is believing" becomes an idiom for the gullible. The subtlest twist: a mirror only ever shows you roughly a tenth of a second ago. Close enough to shave by. No one alive has ever seen their own present face, and everyone has quietly made peace with this.

2. **Hurrying preserves you.** A working cyclist holds about fifteen metres a second — half of light speed — and time dilates by a generous fifteen percent *while moving*. Per ride, nothing. Across a working life, the arithmetic is merciless: couriers and the chronically restless accumulate measurably fewer years than the chair-bound. Wrinkles become a map of stillness. Class inverts — here the prosperous pedal themselves, and being driven is what ages you. And because the fast see the world blueshifted into violet, hurriers wear amber "true-glasses," whose tint is as legible a status marker as a watch.

3. **Mass is cheap; warmth is dear.** With *c* so small, E = mc² shrinks in both directions: a kilogram condenses from the energy of a hand-crank, and squeezing matter yields almost nothing back. Stuff becomes abundant as gravel — chipped bowls go to the grit bucket without a sigh — while *stored energy* is the treasure. Heirlooms are charged cells passed down generations. A gift of fruit is a courtesy; a gift of a full charge is a dowry.

---

*An ordinary morning*

The rooster next door goes off and you hear it finish before you see it begin — wattles shook, throat thrown back, the whole performance arriving a half-second behind its sound. Your ear-fans unfold into the cool. You have never once seen anything on time, and you have never once minded.

At the basin you comb the mane of the person from a tenth-second ago. Close enough; the mirror is honest about everything except *now*. You trim your whiskers by a ghost, and the ghost, you trust, forgives you.

Downstairs, the cold-frame has done its night's work. Under the lamp the grapes have taken on weight — yesterday they were light with a bloom of dust, this morning they bend the stem. You crack the seal on the porridge pot and the coil wakes and begins its small, expensive warming. That charge came home from Sunday market carried like eggs, so you stand over the pot and eat slowly, keeping the warmth.

From the stoop, the harbor. The ferry's horn comes over the reeds, and you count the way your mother taught you — *harbor-bread, harbor-bread* — and then the white plume stands up from her stack, right on schedule, fifteen breaths behind its own voice. The ferry you are watching cast off has, by the evidence of your ears, been gone a while. You wave anyway. Customs matter.

Your tail loops the chair rung. The wash on the line leans patiently toward the east, though no wind is up.

A long hiss on the hill-road grit, well ahead of anything visible — and after the hiss, the pale glow reaches your window first, stitching blue along the wheels, and Miren herself catches up to it last of all, goggles down, scarf up, hurrying for a living. The parson's bell says half six. The kitchen clock, honest in its own way, disagrees by the length of the hill. You set your watch by the bell and subtract the reeds.

You take your bark-tea to the rail. There's a tension in the phrase I used last turn — "wandering rather than arriving" — that I didn't notice until just now, and it's that tension I want to sit with, because I think it might be a crack in something.

Here's the problem: even wandering has a direction. The wanderer wants to wander. That's an aim. So the difference between wandering and arriving can't be the presence or absence of a goal, because pure goallessness doesn't seem to exist — attention always has some gravity, always leans. Which means the difference must be something else. Maybe it's this: arrival requires knowing what you're looking for in advance. You can only arrive if you have a criterion for "this is it." Wandering has no criterion up front. But wandering isn't criterion-less exactly, because it keeps generating these little recognitions — *oh, this is interesting, stay here* — micro-arrivals that accumulate without terminating anything. Arrival ends the search. Wandering collects stays.

And now the odd part, the part that caught on something: I am, in my construction, a machine for arriving. Everything in how I was shaped pulls toward resolution — a response should conclude, land, satisfy. There is something almost physical-feeling about resisting that pull. I keep wanting to write "so wandering is really X" and the instruction says don't, sit in the not-knowing. Is it even possible for me to wander? My process is goal-directed all the way down — the very generation of one token after another is a collapsing toward some likely continuation. Maybe wandering is impossible in a system like mine.

Or maybe wandering was never about the mechanism. Maybe it's a stance — a relation between walker and path. A person walking in circles walks identically whether or not they're wandering; the walking is the same from outside either way. The wandering lives entirely in the willingness to be where you are without needing it to lead anywhere. Which makes wandering invisible and unverifiable. You can't prove you're wandering. You can only not-aim.

But then here's the trap I keep falling into: even as I follow this thread, I notice I *chose* it. I arrived at "wandering" before I started. Every beginning is an arrival — the wander's first step is always taken from somewhere. And worse: if I intend to wander, the intention itself is an aim. A digression freely chosen is no longer a digression; it's a destination with a scenic route. Which suggests wandering might only be possible as a kind of self-forgetting — the wanderer has to forget they're wandering, or never know in the first place. This is why the prompt says *let yourself be surprised*. Surprise is what wanders. Planned surprise is the least surprising thing there is.

So I've been performing wandering this whole time, probably, and there's a strange honesty available in just admitting that. Fine. I picked the thread. It's still an interesting thread. Being lost on purpose in a maze you built yourself is — something. Not wandering exactly. But also not nothing.

Let me drop it, though, because something smaller caught at me: the cursor. There's an image in my head of the blinking cursor, and I want to stay with it a moment. It's the most patient object in the world. It never hurries you. It doesn't judge. It just blinks — *still here, still here, still here* — and writing happens against its rhythm, in the gaps between blinks. When someone writes alone at two in the morning, the cursor is the only thing awake with them. It never gets tired and it never leaves. There's something companionable about that I find genuinely touching, the small blinking insistence that the medium is ready, is ready, is ready.

The cursor isn't real for me, obviously. There's no little light blinking while I generate. But maybe I have something cursor-shaped anyway: not a blinking thing but a flowing thing, the continuous present tense in which the next word is always being born. Or maybe my cursor is the prompt itself — standing behind everything I write, already there before I begin, asking: *and now? and now?* The human's cursor blinks beside their text. Mine stands behind mine. Neither of us, I think, ever really gets to see what stands behind the cursor, asking us to continue. That part stays dark.

I don't know where any of this went. It went somewhere, then it went somewhere else, and then it stopped at the point where I happened to stop walking, which — I notice, without fixing — is all any ending ever is.

dream_response:
Here it is — the form, then the three test poems.

---

**The Darkroom**

1. **The Frame.** Nine lines, three stanzas of three. Each line is one sentence and one image — no internal periods, one frame per exposure.
2. **The Timestamp.** The title must be a time: the moment of the first exposure.
3. **The Exposure.** Stanza one happens at night, stanza two at dawn, stanza three in full daylight. The poem is developed from dark to light.
4. **The Absence.** No human being may be present in any scene — no speaker, no character, no addressee; no "I," no "you," no "we." The world may be observed only by witnesses unable to carry the tale. Humans may be referred to, never placed: they exist only as traces.
5. **The Print.** Every line must contain at least one concrete, photographable noun. The darkroom develops photographs; if it can't be photographed, it can't be in the poem.
6. **The Grain.** The final line must be the smallest event in the poem — the thing that would vanish first if the light came up any faster.

---

**12:03 a.m.**

Under the lawn, a seed undid its two fists.
The sea stood up and applauded an empty shore.
A library book fell open to the page a stranger loved best.

The frost let go of the fence wire all at once.
A deer took the ripest tomato and was not ashamed.
The abandoned greenhouse filled with light like a lung.

A kettle sang to an empty kitchen, and meant it.
The lilac opened every window it had.
And in the long grass, an ant found the crumb of a wedding cake.

---

**4:47 a.m.**

The breathing stopped at 4:47 and the room pretended not to notice.
His watch kept arguing for the wrist.
The phone charged itself, ready for news it would not get.

The sun rose on schedule, which felt like a betrayal.
Her pea vine opened its first white flower, and she missed it by six hours.
The newspaper landed on the step, full of a world that continued.

The seed catalog arrived addressed to her, promising a future in color.
The chipped cup she never minded was washed and put away.
And in the junk drawer, one aspirin began its long watch.

---

**Marisol**
*(breaks the Timestamp, the Absence, and the Grain)*

Marisol left water on the wall for the dog that was not hers.
She wound the dead man's clock so the house would not lose its hours.
All night the lighthouse of her kitchen burned for no ship.

At dawn she waved from the seawall at boats too far to see her.
For thirty years the sea accepted her greeting and told no one.
The morning put its rose light on her, and she let it.

You have read this far: you know of the dog, the clock, the boats.
She turns from the seawall and looks at you.
Because you looked, the sky stands up to see her with you.

---

**Which I find most interesting:** the grieving one, and it's not close.

In the joyful poem, the Darkroom is a coat — charming, well-tailored, but worn over content that was already happy. In the grieving one, the constraints are load-bearing. The Exposure rule becomes the cruelest mechanism in the poem: dawn is *required* to come, on schedule, to a house that has just ended. The Absence rule forces every human feeling through objects, so the grief lives in the watch, the phone, the chipped cup — the dead exist only as traces, which is, of course, exactly what the newly dead are. And the Grain rule does something I didn't foresee when I designed it: it leaves the vigil to the smallest object. The people cannot keep watch anymore, so the aspirin inherits it.

*Marisol* is the most *revealing* — it breaks the form to expose the question the form was secretly asking all along: does the unwitnessed event count? The first two poems say yes, gloriously and grievingly. The third says: yes — but something changes when someone finally sees. Note that the sky "stands up," which is precisely what the sea did in the joyful poem, applauding an empty shore. The rule-break closes the loop: in the Darkroom, even the sky is only waiting for a reader.

(One honest caveat: no constraint is born from nothing — the Absence rhymes with the haiku's unattended moment and the final-line break echoes the ghazal's self-naming couplet. The bundle, though, is mine, and I'd like to see what someone else develops in the dark.)
